issues.legal_issue: The death of one among multiple plaintiffs with separate shares does not abate the entire appeal when the surviving plaintiffs substantially represent the deceased plaintiff’s interest.
material_facts: Several plaintiffs brought the suit as successors claiming shares in the same estate.
One plaintiff died while the appeal was pending in the High Court, and that plaintiff’s legal representatives were not substituted.
The surviving plaintiffs had definite shares in the estate and continued the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The appeal did not abate as a whole; the surviving plaintiffs were entitled to proceed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXII Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, where the right to sue survives to the remaining plaintiffs, the proceedings may continue. Whether an appeal abates in its entirety depends on the circumstances, particularly whether the remaining parties’ decree could be contradictory or inconsistent with a decree concerning the deceased party. The Court applied Budh Ram v. Bansi (2010) 11 SCC 476, Sardar Amarjit Singh Kalra v. Pramod Gupta (2003) 3 SCC 72, Harihar Singh v. Balmiki Prasad Singh (1976) 1 SCC 212, and State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram (1962) 2 SCR 636.

predicates.multiple_plaintiff_appeal: Multiple plaintiffs brought or continued an appeal arising from the same suit.
predicates.plaintiff_dies_during_appeal: One plaintiff died while the appeal was pending and that plaintiff’s legal representatives were not substituted.
predicates.surviving_sharers_represent_estate: The surviving plaintiffs held distinct shares in the estate and substantially represented the deceased plaintiff’s interest.

issues.definition: When multiple plaintiffs appeal, one dies without substitution, and the surviving sharers represent the estate, the appeal continues rather than abating as a whole.

issues.legal_issue: A reference to a third judge under the applicable Letters Patent procedure is not invalid merely because the differing judges did not jointly formulate their points of disagreement before the reference.
material_facts: A civil appeal was heard by a two-judge bench governed by the applicable Letters Patent procedure.
The judges delivered separate judgments that differed on facts and law.
The Chief Justice referred the appeal to a third judge, who considered the separate judgments, formulated issues, and decided the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The reference and the third judge’s decision complied with the applicable Letters Patent procedure and were not invalid for want of a joint formulation of the points of disagreement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 98(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure preserves provisions of a High Court’s Letters Patent. Clause 36 of the Letters Patent applicable to the High Court governed the procedure where judges differed, and permitted a third judge to hear and decide the matter. The Court relied on Reliance Industries Ltd. v. Pravinbhai Jasbhai Patel (1997) 7 SCC 300 and distinguished Tej Kaur v. Kirpal Singh (1995) 5 SCC 119, P.V. Hemalatha v. Kattamkandi Puthiya Maliackal Saheeda (2002) 5 SCC 548, and Pankajakshi v. Chandrika (2010) 13 SCC 303, which concerned courts not governed by the relevant Letters Patent procedure.

predicates.civil_appeal_before_letters_patent_court: A civil appeal was heard in a High Court whose procedure was governed by an applicable Letters Patent provision.
predicates.two_judges_differ: The judges hearing the appeal delivered separate judgments that differed on matters in the appeal.
predicates.third_judge_considers_separate_judgments: The appeal was referred to a third judge, who considered the differing judgments and determined the issues.

issues.definition: Where a civil appeal is governed by Letters Patent procedure, differing judges’ separate judgments may be considered by a third judge without a prior joint formulation of their disagreements.

issues.legal_issue: Successors may establish ownership and obtain correction of land records when authoritative land records identify their predecessor as pattadar or owner, succession is shown, and the State fails to prove lawful confiscation or vesting of the land.
material_facts: The land records, including the survey and settlement records and the Khasra Pahani, recorded the predecessor as pattadar or owner and identified the land as self-cultivated.
Documents evidenced succession from the predecessor to the plaintiffs.
Maps and plans supported the identity of the land despite inconsistent or duplicated survey-number entries.
The State did not produce a proceeding or order establishing confiscation or vesting of the land, or explain how the land came to be recorded as government land.
Evidence and the State’s admissions supported the plaintiffs’ possession; the State had transferred the land to a corporation during the pending High Court appeal.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs established their predecessors’ title and their succession to it. The decree for correction of the land records and protection of their possession was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Regulation 13 of the Hyderabad (Telangana Area) Record-of-Rights in Land Regulation, 1358 Fasli, provided that an entry in the record of rights was presumed true until the contrary was proved. The Court relied on Collector v. Narsing Rao (2015) 3 SCC 695, which described the Khasra as a historical record that could serve as a deed of title when no other title deed existed. Sections 17 and 18 of the Hyderabad (Abolition of Jagirs) Regulation, 1358 Fasli, preserved qualifying home-farms and personal property from the effect of abolition; Jagir status alone did not establish that this land had vested in the State. The Court distinguished State of Himachal Pradesh v. Keshav Ram, AIR 1997 SC 2181, because there the State had been recorded as owner, whereas the relevant record here identified the predecessor as owner.

rule.if: successors_seek_record_correction and predecessor_recorded_as_owner and succession_evidenced and land_identity_supported and state_lacks_proof_of_lawful_vesting

predicates.successors_seek_record_correction: Persons claiming through a predecessor sought recognition of their interest and correction of land records.
predicates.predecessor_recorded_as_owner: Land records prepared through survey or settlement identified the predecessor as pattadar, owner, or self-cultivator of the land.
predicates.succession_evidenced: Documents or other evidence showed that the claimants succeeded to the predecessor’s interest.
predicates.land_identity_supported: Maps, plans, or consistent land records supported the identity of the claimed parcel despite inconsistent entries or survey numbers.
predicates.state_lacks_proof_of_lawful_vesting: The State produced no competent order or proceeding establishing confiscation or vesting of the identified land in the State.

issues.definition: When successors seeking correction rely on land records identifying their predecessor as owner, evidence their succession, establish the parcel’s identity, and the State fails to prove lawful vesting, they are entitled to recognition of their interest and correction of the records.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee that acquires disputed property while an appeal concerning it is pending takes subject to the litigation and cannot obtain success in its appeal merely by virtue of the transfer.
material_facts: The State transferred the suit land to a corporation while the appeal concerning the land was pending in the High Court.
The corporation appealed against the judgment in favour of the plaintiffs.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was hit by lis pendens, and the corporation’s appeal was dismissed following dismissal of the State’s appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of lis pendens applies to a transfer of property made while litigation concerning that property is pending. The Court also relied on the consequence of dismissing the transferor State’s appeal when dismissing the transferee corporation’s appeal.

predicates.property_appeal_pending: An appeal concerning rights to particular property was pending.
predicates.property_transferred_during_appeal: A party to the dispute transferred the property while that appeal was pending.
predicates.transferor_appeal_dismissed: The appeal brought by the party that transferred the property was dismissed.

issues.definition: When property is transferred during a pending appeal and the transferor’s appeal is dismissed, the transferee’s appeal is also dismissed.
